sections.title: Section A — common to Mathematics and Applied Mathematics (compulsory)

questions.topic: Algebra: Matrices, Determinants, Inverse and the Matrix Method
questions.question: If \(\begin{bmatrix}x + y&2\\5&x - y\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}6&2\\5&2\end{bmatrix}\), then:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(x = 4, y = 2\)
Given: equal matrices have equal corresponding entries
Formula: \(x + y = 6\), \(x - y = 2\)
Step 1: Adding: \(2x = 8 \Rightarrow x = 4\)
Step 2: \(y = 6 - 4 = 2\)
Common mistake: (A) swaps \(x\) and \(y\). (B) uses only \(x + y = 6\).
Key point: Compare entry by entry.

questions.question: The area of the region bounded by \(y = \sqrt{x}\), the \(x\)-axis and the line \(x = 4\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\dfrac{16}{3}\) sq units
Given: \(y = \sqrt{x} \ge 0\) on \([0, 4]\)
Formula: Area \(= \int_0^4 x^{1/2}dx\)
Step 1: \(\left[\dfrac{2}{3}x^{3/2}\right]_0^4 = \dfrac{2}{3} \times 8\)
Step 2: \(= \dfrac{16}{3}\)
Common mistake: \(\dfrac{8}{3}\) (A) uses \(\dfrac{1}{3}\) in place of \(\dfrac{2}{3}\). \(8\) (B) forgets the factor \(\dfrac{2}{3}\).
Key point: \(4^{3/2} = (\sqrt{4})^3 = 8\).

questions.question: \(\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4}\sec^2 x\,dx\) equals:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(1\)
Given: limits \(0\) and \(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\)
Formula: \(\int \sec^2 x\,dx = \tan x\)
Step 1: \([\tan x]_0^{\pi/4} = 1 - 0 = 1\)
Common mistake: \(\sqrt{2}\) (C) uses \(\sec\dfrac{\pi}{4}\) in place of \(\tan\dfrac{\pi}{4}\).
Key point: \(\tan x\) is the antiderivative of \(\sec^2 x\).

questions.topic: Algebra: Matrices, Determinants, Inverse and the Matrix Method
questions.question:
For \(A = \begin{bmatrix}1&2\\2&3\end{bmatrix}\), consider the following statements:
(A) \(A\) is symmetric.
(B) \(|A| = -1\).
(C) \(A\) is invertible.
(D) \(A^T = -A\).
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) \(a_{12} = a_{21} = 2\). (B) \(3 - 4 = -1\). (C) \(|A| \ne 0\), so \(A^{-1}\) exists.
Why not the others: (D) is false: \(A^T = A\), and \(-A\) has negative diagonal entries. Options (C) and (D) include (D); (A) leaves out (C).
Key point: A matrix is invertible exactly when its determinant is non-zero.

questions.sub_topic: A distribution with P(X = x) = kx
questions.question:
A random variable \(X\) takes the values 1, 2, 3, 4 with \(P(X = x) = kx\). Consider the following statements:
(A) \(k = 0.1\)
(B) \(P(X \le 2) = 0.3\)
(C) \(E(X) = 3\)
(D) \(P(X = 4) = 0.3\)
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (D) only
Why: \(k(1 + 2 + 3 + 4) = 1 \Rightarrow k = 0.1\). Only (D) is false: \(P(X = 4) = 4k = 0.4\).
Why not the others: (B) \(0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3\). (C) \(E(X) = 0.1 + 0.4 + 0.9 + 1.6 = 3\). Options (A), (C) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: Find \(k\) from the total probability first.

questions.sub_topic: Four differential equations and their solutions
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Differential equation)
(A) \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 2x\)
(B) \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = y\)
(C) \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\dfrac{x}{y}\)
(D) \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{1}{x}\)

List-II (General solution)
(I) \(y = Ce^x\)
(II) \(x^2 + y^2 = C\)
(III) \(y = \log|x| + C\)
(IV) \(y = x^2 + C\)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(IV), (B)-(I), (C)-(II), (D)-(III)
Step 1: \(\int 2x\,dx = x^2 + C\) (IV)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{dy}{y} = dx \Rightarrow \log|y| = x + c \Rightarrow y = Ce^x\) (I)
Step 3: \(y\,dy = -x\,dx \Rightarrow \dfrac{y^2}{2} = -\dfrac{x^2}{2} + c \Rightarrow x^2 + y^2 = C\) (II)
Step 4: \(\int \dfrac{dx}{x} = \log|x| + C\) (III)
Common mistake: (A) swaps the first two. (B) swaps \(y = Ce^x\) and the circle. (C) swaps the last two.
Key point: Separate the variables, then integrate both sides.

questions.question: \(\displaystyle\int x\sqrt{x}\,dx\) equals:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\dfrac{2}{5}x^{5/2} + C\)
Given: \(x\sqrt{x} = x^{3/2}\)
Formula: \(\int x^n dx = \dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} + C\)
Step 1: \(n + 1 = \dfrac{5}{2}\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{x^{5/2}}{5/2} = \dfrac{2}{5}x^{5/2} + C\)
Common mistake: (A) differentiates \(x^{3/2}\). (C) multiplies by \(\dfrac{5}{2}\) instead of dividing. (D) integrates \(\sqrt{x}\) alone.
Key point: Write roots as fractional powers first.

questions.topic: Calculus: Derivatives, Increasing/Decreasing Functions, Maxima and Minima
questions.question: The local minimum value of \(f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 + 4\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(0\)
Given: \(f'(x) = 3x^2 - 6x = 3x(x - 2)\); \(f''(x) = 6x - 6\)
Formula: local minimum where \(f' = 0\) and \(f'' > 0\)
Step 1: \(f''(2) = 6 > 0\), so \(x = 2\) gives the local minimum
Step 2: \(f(2) = 8 - 12 + 4 = 0\)
Common mistake: \(4\) (A) is the local maximum value \(f(0)\). \(2\) (B) is the point, not the value.
Key point: Use \(f''\) to tell the maximum from the minimum.

questions.question: The maximum value of \(Z = 2x + 3y\) subject to \(x + y \le 5\), \(x \le 3\), \(y \le 4\), \(x, y \ge 0\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(14\)
Given: constraints \(x + y \le 5\), \(x \le 3\), \(y \le 4\), \(x, y \ge 0\)
Formula: evaluate \(Z\) at every corner
Step 1: Corners: \((0, 0)\), \((3, 0)\), \((3, 2)\), \((1, 4)\), \((0, 4)\)
Step 2: \(Z = 0, 6, 12, 14, 12\)
Step 3: Maximum \(Z = 14\) at \((1, 4)\)
Common mistake: \(15\) (B) uses \((0, 5)\), which breaks \(y \le 4\). \(12\) (A) stops at \((3, 2)\) or \((0, 4)\).
Key point: Every constraint can cut off a corner; list them all.

questions.topic: Algebra: Matrices, Determinants, Inverse and the Matrix Method
questions.question: The value of \(\begin{vmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{vmatrix}\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(1\)
Given: \(a = \cos\theta\), \(b = -\sin\theta\), \(c = \sin\theta\), \(d = \cos\theta\)
Formula: \(ad - bc\)
Step 1: \(\cos^2\theta - (-\sin\theta)(\sin\theta) = \cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1\)
Common mistake: \(\cos 2\theta\) (B) forgets the minus sign in \(b\), giving \(\cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta\).
Key point: The two minus signs make \(+\sin^2\theta\).

questions.question: A bag has 5 red and 3 blue balls. Two balls are drawn one after the other without replacement. The probability that both are red is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\dfrac{5}{14}\)
Given: 8 balls, 5 red
Formula: \(P(R_1 \cap R_2) = P(R_1)P(R_2 \mid R_1)\)
Step 1: \(P(R_1) = \dfrac{5}{8}\); then 4 red remain out of 7, so \(P(R_2 \mid R_1) = \dfrac{4}{7}\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{5}{8} \times \dfrac{4}{7} = \dfrac{20}{56} = \dfrac{5}{14}\)
Common mistake: \(\dfrac{25}{64}\) (A) replaces the first ball. \(\dfrac{5}{8}\) (B) is the first draw only.
Key point: Without replacement, the second probability changes.

questions.sub_topic: Value of a growth solution at x = 1
questions.question: The solution of \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 2y\) with \(y(0) = 3\) gives \(y(1)\) equal to:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(3e^2\)
Given: \(\dfrac{dy}{y} = 2\,dx\), \(y(0) = 3\)
Formula: \(\log|y| = 2x + c \Rightarrow y = Ce^{2x}\)
Step 1: \(y(0) = C = 3\), so \(y = 3e^{2x}\)
Step 2: \(y(1) = 3e^2\)
Common mistake: \(e^2\) (B) forgets the constant \(C = 3\). \(3e\) (C) drops the 2 in the exponent.
Key point: Use the initial condition to fix the constant.

questions.topic: Calculus: Derivatives, Increasing/Decreasing Functions, Maxima and Minima
questions.question: If \(y = \sin 3x\), then \(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(-9\sin 3x\)
Given: \(y = \sin 3x\)
Formula: chain rule twice
Step 1: \(y' = 3\cos 3x\)
Step 2: \(y'' = -9\sin 3x\)
Common mistake: (D) is the first derivative. (A) loses the minus sign from differentiating cosine.
Key point: Each differentiation brings out a factor 3.

questions.topic: Algebra: Matrices, Determinants, Inverse and the Matrix Method
questions.question: \(A\) and \(B\) are square matrices of order 3 with \(|A| = 2\) and \(|B| = 3\). Then \(|2AB^T|\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(48\)
Given: \(n = 3\), \(|A| = 2\), \(|B^T| = |B| = 3\)
Formula: \(|kM| = k^n|M|\), \(|AB^T| = |A||B^T|\)
Step 1: \(|AB^T| = 2 \times 3 = 6\)
Step 2: \(|2AB^T| = 2^3 \times 6 = 48\)
Common mistake: \(12\) (B) uses \(2 \times 6\) instead of \(2^3 \times 6\). \(96\) (D) uses \(2^4\).
Key point: Transposing does not change a determinant.

questions.topic: Calculus: Derivatives, Increasing/Decreasing Functions, Maxima and Minima
questions.sub_topic: Smallest sum of squares with a fixed sum
questions.question: Two positive numbers add up to 16. The smallest possible value of the sum of their squares is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(128\)
Given: numbers \(x\) and \(16 - x\)
Formula: \(S(x) = x^2 + (16 - x)^2\); \(S'(x) = 0\), \(S'' > 0\)
Step 1: \(S'(x) = 2x - 2(16 - x) = 4x - 32 = 0 \Rightarrow x = 8\)
Step 2: \(S''(x) = 4 > 0\), so this is a minimum
Step 3: \(S(8) = 64 + 64 = 128\)
Common mistake: \(64\) (B) squares only one of the numbers. \(136\) (C) tries 6 and 10 instead of finding the minimum.
Key point: The sum of squares is least when the two numbers are equal.

questions.sub_topic: Bayes' theorem for a medical test
questions.question: A disease affects 1% of a population. A test is positive for 90% of people who have it and for 10% of people who do not. A person tests positive. The probability that the person has the disease is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(\dfrac{1}{12}\)
Given: \(P(D) = 0.01\), \(P(+ \mid D) = 0.9\); \(P(D') = 0.99\), \(P(+ \mid D') = 0.1\)
Formula: \(P(D \mid +) = \dfrac{P(D)P(+ \mid D)}{P(D)P(+ \mid D) + P(D')P(+ \mid D')}\)
Step 1: Numerator \(= 0.01 \times 0.9 = 0.009\)
Step 2: Denominator \(= 0.009 + 0.99 \times 0.1 = 0.009 + 0.099 = 0.108\)
Step 3: \(P(D \mid +) = \dfrac{0.009}{0.108} = \dfrac{1}{12}\)
Common mistake: \(\dfrac{9}{10}\) (A) confuses \(P(+ \mid D)\) with \(P(D \mid +)\). \(\dfrac{1}{11}\) (B) uses 0.1 in place of 0.099 in the denominator.
Key point: When a disease is rare, most positive results come from healthy people.

questions.topic: Unit III: Applications of the Integrals
questions.sub_topic: Regions bounded by an ellipse and by lines
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The area enclosed by \(\dfrac{x^2}{16} + \dfrac{y^2}{9} = 1\) is \(12\pi\) sq units.
(B) The part of that ellipse in the first quadrant has area \(3\pi\) sq units.
(C) The region enclosed by that ellipse is symmetric about both axes.
(D) The area bounded by \(y = |x|\) and \(y = 1\) is \(2\) sq units.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) \(\pi ab = \pi(4)(3) = 12\pi\). (B) one quarter of \(12\pi\) is \(3\pi\). (C) replacing \(x\) by \(-x\) or \(y\) by \(-y\) leaves the equation unchanged.
Why not the others: (D) is false: the region is a triangle with vertices \((0, 0)\), \((\pm 1, 1)\), so its area is \(\dfrac{1}{2} \times 2 \times 1 = 1\). Options (C) and (D) include (D); (B) leaves out (C).
Key point: Symmetry reduces an area to one quadrant.

questions.sub_topic: Is x times the modulus of x a bijection?
questions.question: The function \(f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\), \(f(x) = x|x|\), is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Both one-one and onto
Why: \(f(x) = x^2\) for \(x \ge 0\) and \(f(x) = -x^2\) for \(x < 0\). It is strictly increasing on \(\mathbb{R}\), so it is one-one, and it takes every real value (\(\sqrt{y}\) for \(y \ge 0\), \(-\sqrt{-y}\) for \(y < 0\)), so it is onto.
Why not the others: (A) misses negative outputs from negative inputs. (B) and (D) treat it like \(x^2\), but \(f(-2) = -4 \ne f(2) = 4\).
Key point: Split a modulus function into cases before testing it.

questions.sub_topic: Number of reflexive relations on three elements
questions.question: How many of the relations on \(\{a, b, c\}\) are reflexive?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(64\)
Given: \(A \times A\) has 9 pairs, 3 of them diagonal
Formula: the 3 diagonal pairs must be included; each of the other \(9 - 3 = 6\) pairs is free
Step 1: \(2^6 = 64\)
Common mistake: \(512\) (A) is \(2^9\), the number of all relations.
Key point: Reflexive relations on \(n\) elements number \(2^{n^2 - n}\).

questions.sub_topic: Integration by parts: x sin x on [0, π]
questions.question: \(\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi}x\sin x\,dx\) equals:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(\pi\)
Given: \(u = x\), \(dv = \sin x\,dx\); \(du = dx\), \(v = -\cos x\)
Formula: \(\int_a^b u\,dv = [uv]_a^b - \int_a^b v\,du\)
Step 1: \([-x\cos x]_0^{\pi} = -\pi\cos\pi + 0 = \pi\)
Step 2: \(\int_0^{\pi}\cos x\,dx = [\sin x]_0^{\pi} = 0\)
Step 3: Total \(= \pi + 0 = \pi\)
Common mistake: \(2\) (B) is \(\int_0^{\pi}\sin x\,dx\), ignoring the factor \(x\). \(0\) (A) takes \(\cos\pi = 1\).
Key point: \(\cos\pi = -1\).

questions.sub_topic: Condition for a unique solution of a 3 × 3 system
questions.question: The system \(x + y + z = 1\), \(x + 2y + 3z = 2\), \(x + 3y + \lambda z = 3\) has a unique solution when:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\lambda \ne 5\)
Given: coefficient matrix \(A = \begin{bmatrix}1&1&1\\1&2&3\\1&3&\lambda\end{bmatrix}\)
Formula: unique solution when \(|A| \ne 0\)
Step 1: \(|A| = 1(2\lambda - 9) - 1(\lambda - 3) + 1(3 - 2)\)
Step 2: \(= 2\lambda - 9 - \lambda + 3 + 1 = \lambda - 5\)
Step 3: \(|A| \ne 0 \iff \lambda \ne 5\)
Common mistake: (A) gives the value where the solution is not unique. (C) takes \(\lambda\) equal to the entry above it.
Key point: A non-zero determinant means exactly one solution.

questions.sub_topic: Angles for four pairs of lines
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Direction ratios of two lines)
(A) \(1, 0, 0\) and \(0, 1, 0\)
(B) \(1, 1, 0\) and \(1, 0, 0\)
(C) \(1, 1, 1\) and \(2, 2, 2\)
(D) \(1, 0, 0\) and \(1, \sqrt{3}, 0\)

List-II (Angle between the lines)
(I) \(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\)
(II) \(0\)
(III) \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\)
(IV) \(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
Formula: \(\cos\theta = \dfrac{|a_1a_2 + b_1b_2 + c_1c_2|}{\sqrt{a_1^2 + b_1^2 + c_1^2}\sqrt{a_2^2 + b_2^2 + c_2^2}}\)
Step 1: (A) numerator 0, so \(\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\) (III)
Step 2: (B) \(\cos\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\), so \(\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\) (IV)
Step 3: (C) the ratios are proportional, so the lines are parallel: \(\theta = 0\) (II)
Step 4: (D) \(\cos\theta = \dfrac{1}{1 \times 2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\), so \(\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\) (I)
Common mistake: (B) swaps the first two. (C) swaps the parallel pair with the \(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\) pair. (D) swaps the last two.
Key point: Proportional direction ratios mean parallel lines.

questions.question: The shortest distance between the lines \(\vec{r} = (\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + \hat{k}) + \lambda(\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k})\) and \(\vec{r} = (2\hat{i} - \hat{j} - \hat{k}) + \mu(2\hat{i} + \hat{j} + 2\hat{k})\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{2}}\)
Given: \(\vec{b}_1 = (1, -1, 1)\), \(\vec{b}_2 = (2, 1, 2)\), \(\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1 = (1, -3, -2)\)
Formula: \(d = \dfrac{|(\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2)\cdot(\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1)|}{|\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2|}\)
Step 1: \(\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2 = \begin{vmatrix}\hat{i}&\hat{j}&\hat{k}\\1&-1&1\\2&1&2\end{vmatrix} = (-2 - 1)\hat{i} - (2 - 2)\hat{j} + (1 + 2)\hat{k} = -3\hat{i} + 3\hat{k}\)
Step 2: \(|\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2| = 3\sqrt{2}\); dot with \((1, -3, -2)\): \(-3 + 0 - 6 = -9\)
Step 3: \(d = \dfrac{9}{3\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{2}}\)
Common mistake: \(9\) (A) forgets to divide by \(|\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2|\). (D) inverts the fraction.
Key point: Distance = |scalar triple product| ÷ |cross product of the directions|.

questions.question:
For events with \(P(A) = 0.6\), \(P(B) = 0.3\) and \(P(A \cap B) = 0.2\), consider the following statements:
(A) \(P(A \cup B) = 0.7\)
(B) \(P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{2}{3}\)
(C) \(P(B \mid A) = \dfrac{1}{3}\)
(D) \(A\) and \(B\) are independent.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (D) only
Why: Only (D) is false: \(P(A)P(B) = 0.18 \ne 0.2\).
Why not the others: (A) \(0.6 + 0.3 - 0.2 = 0.7\). (B) \(\dfrac{0.2}{0.3} = \dfrac{2}{3}\). (C) \(\dfrac{0.2}{0.6} = \dfrac{1}{3}\). Options (B), (C) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: Independence needs \(P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)\) exactly.

questions.sub_topic: Degree after clearing a fractional power
questions.question: The degree of the differential equation \(\left[1 + \left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^2\right]^{3/2} = \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(2\)
Given: the equation contains a fractional power
Formula: make it polynomial in the derivatives first
Step 1: Square both sides: \(\left[1 + \left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^2\right]^3 = \left(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\right)^2\)
Step 2: The highest derivative \(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\) now has power 2, so the degree is 2
Common mistake: \(\dfrac{3}{2}\) (A) reads the degree before clearing the fractional power. \(3\) (B) takes the power of the first-order term.
Key point: Degree is defined only after the equation is polynomial in its derivatives.

questions.sub_topic: Minimum on an unbounded region with two constraints
questions.question: The minimum value of \(Z = 3x + 5y\) subject to \(x + 3y \ge 3\), \(x + y \ge 2\), \(x, y \ge 0\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(7\)
Given: unbounded feasible region
Formula: evaluate \(Z\) at the corners, then check the half-plane \(Z <\) smallest value
Step 1: Corners: \((3, 0)\), \((0, 2)\) and the intersection of \(x + 3y = 3\), \(x + y = 2\): \(2y = 1\), \(y = 0.5\), \(x = 1.5\)
Step 2: \(Z(3, 0) = 9\), \(Z(1.5, 0.5) = 4.5 + 2.5 = 7\), \(Z(0, 2) = 10\)
Step 3: \(3x + 5y < 7\) has no point in common with the region, so the minimum is 7
Common mistake: \(9\) (A) checks only the corners on the axes. \(6\) (C) uses \((2, 0)\), which breaks \(x + 3y \ge 3\).
Key point: For an unbounded region, confirm the minimum with the half-plane test.

questions.question: \(\displaystyle\int \dfrac{dx}{x\log x}\) equals:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\log|\log x| + C\)
Given: put \(t = \log x\), \(dt = \dfrac{dx}{x}\)
Formula: \(\int \dfrac{dt}{t} = \log|t| + C\)
Step 1: \(\int \dfrac{dt}{t} = \log|\log x| + C\)
Common mistake: (C) is \(\int \dfrac{\log x}{x}dx\). (A) ignores the \(\log x\) in the denominator.
Key point: \(\dfrac{1}{x}\) is the derivative of \(\log x\), so substitute \(t = \log x\).

questions.question: \(\displaystyle\int e^x(\sin x + \cos x)\,dx\) equals:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(e^x\sin x + C\)
Given: \(f(x) = \sin x\), \(f'(x) = \cos x\)
Formula: \(\int e^x[f(x) + f'(x)]\,dx = e^xf(x) + C\)
Step 1: \(e^x\sin x + C\)
Step 2: Check: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}(e^x\sin x) = e^x\sin x + e^x\cos x\) ✓
Common mistake: (A) takes \(f = \cos x\), but \((\cos x)' = -\sin x\), not \(\sin x\).
Key point: Spot which term is the derivative of the other.

questions.sub_topic: Line equally inclined to the axes
questions.question: A line makes equal acute angles with the three coordinate axes. Its direction cosines are:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}, \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}, \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\)
Given: \(l = m = n\), all positive (acute angles)
Formula: \(l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1\)
Step 1: \(3l^2 = 1 \Rightarrow l = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\)
Common mistake: (A) gives direction ratios, not cosines. (C) uses \(3l = 1\) instead of \(3l^2 = 1\).
Key point: The squares of the direction cosines add up to 1.

questions.question: If \(y = x^x\) (\(x > 0\)), then \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\) at \(x = 1\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(1\)
Given: \(\log y = x\log x\)
Formula: logarithmic differentiation
Step 1: \(\dfrac{1}{y}\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \log x + 1\), so \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = x^x(1 + \log x)\)
Step 2: At \(x = 1\): \(1 \times (1 + 0) = 1\)
Common mistake: \(0\) (A) keeps only the \(\log x\) term. \(2\) (D) takes \(\log 1 = 1\).
Key point: \(\log 1 = 0\).

questions.question: For \(A = \begin{bmatrix}2&1\\3&4\end{bmatrix}\), the product \(A(\text{adj}\,A)\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(\begin{bmatrix}5&0\\0&5\end{bmatrix}\)
Given: \(|A| = 8 - 3 = 5\)
Formula: \(A(\text{adj}\,A) = |A|\,I\)
Step 1: \(5I = \begin{bmatrix}5&0\\0&5\end{bmatrix}\)
Common mistake: (B) is \(AA^{-1}\). (D) is \(\text{adj}\,A\) itself.
Key point: \(A(\text{adj}\,A) = (\text{adj}\,A)A = |A|\,I\).

questions.question: If \(A = \begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&3\end{bmatrix}\), then \(A^3\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\begin{bmatrix}8&0\\0&27\end{bmatrix}\)
Given: \(A\) is diagonal
Formula: powers of a diagonal matrix act on each diagonal entry
Step 1: \(2^3 = 8\), \(3^3 = 27\)
Common mistake: (A) multiplies by 3 instead of cubing.
Key point: \(\text{diag}(a, b)^n = \text{diag}(a^n, b^n)\).

questions.sub_topic: Dot product of two space vectors
questions.question: For \(\vec{a} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k}\) and \(\vec{b} = \hat{i} + \hat{j} - \hat{k}\), \(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(0\)
Given: \(\vec{a} = (2, -1, 1)\), \(\vec{b} = (1, 1, -1)\)
Formula: \(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = a_1b_1 + a_2b_2 + a_3b_3\)
Step 1: \(2 - 1 - 1 = 0\)
Common mistake: \(4\) (C) ignores the minus signs.
Key point: A zero dot product means the vectors are perpendicular.

questions.sub_topic: Inverse functions applied to values outside the branch
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) \(\sin^{-1}\left(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{6}\)
(B) \(\cos^{-1}\left(\cos\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\right) = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}\)
(C) \(\tan^{-1}\left(\tan\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right) = -\dfrac{\pi}{4}\)
(D) \(\sin^{-1}x\) is defined for \(x = 2\).
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) \(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\) is in \(\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\). (B) \(\cos\dfrac{4\pi}{3} = -\dfrac{1}{2}\) and \(\cos^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}\). (C) \(\tan\dfrac{3\pi}{4} = -1\) and \(\tan^{-1}(-1) = -\dfrac{\pi}{4}\).
Why not the others: (D) is false: the domain of \(\sin^{-1}\) is \([-1, 1]\). Option (C) includes (D); (A) and (B) leave out true statements.
Key point: \(f^{-1}(f(x)) = x\) only when \(x\) lies in the principal branch.

questions.question: On the set of all lines in a plane, the relation "\(l_1\) is parallel to \(l_2\)" (a line being taken as parallel to itself) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) An equivalence relation
Why: Every line is parallel to itself (reflexive); if \(l_1 \parallel l_2\) then \(l_2 \parallel l_1\) (symmetric); if \(l_1 \parallel l_2\) and \(l_2 \parallel l_3\) then \(l_1 \parallel l_3\) (transitive).
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) each deny a property the relation has.
Key point: "Is perpendicular to" fails to be reflexive and transitive; "is parallel to" has all three properties.

questions.question: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^2e^x)\) equals:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(e^x(x^2 + 2x)\)
Given: \(u = x^2\), \(v = e^x\)
Formula: \((uv)' = u'v + uv'\)
Step 1: \(2x\cdot e^x + x^2\cdot e^x = e^x(x^2 + 2x)\)
Common mistake: (A) multiplies the two derivatives. (B) keeps only the second term.
Key point: The product rule has two terms.

questions.question: The range of \(f(x) = 2\sin^{-1}x + \dfrac{\pi}{2}\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right]\)
Given: \(-\dfrac{\pi}{2} \le \sin^{-1}x \le \dfrac{\pi}{2}\)
Formula: multiply by 2, then add \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\)
Step 1: \(-\pi \le 2\sin^{-1}x \le \pi\)
Step 2: \(-\dfrac{\pi}{2} \le 2\sin^{-1}x + \dfrac{\pi}{2} \le \dfrac{3\pi}{2}\)
Common mistake: \([-\pi, \pi]\) (C) forgets to add \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\). (D) is the range of \(\sin^{-1}x\) itself.
Key point: Transform the range step by step.

questions.question: The function \(f(x) = e^x - x\) is strictly increasing on:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \((0, \infty)\)
Given: \(f'(x) = e^x - 1\)
Formula: increasing where \(f'(x) > 0\)
Step 1: \(e^x - 1 > 0 \iff e^x > 1 \iff x > 0\)
Common mistake: (B) assumes \(e^x\) dominates everywhere; but \(f'(x) < 0\) for \(x < 0\). (D) solves \(e^x > e\).
Key point: \(e^x > 1\) exactly when \(x > 0\).

questions.question: The general solution of \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{1 + y^2}{1 + x^2}\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\tan^{-1}y = \tan^{-1}x + C\)
Given: \(\dfrac{dy}{1 + y^2} = \dfrac{dx}{1 + x^2}\)
Formula: \(\int \dfrac{dt}{1 + t^2} = \tan^{-1}t\)
Step 1: \(\tan^{-1}y = \tan^{-1}x + C\)
Common mistake: (C) moves the term across with the wrong sign. (D) integrates \(\dfrac{1}{1 + t^2}\) as a logarithm.
Key point: Separate first; each side is then a standard integral.

questions.question: The solution of \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} + y = e^{-x}\) with \(y(0) = 1\) gives \(y(1)\) equal to:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(\dfrac{2}{e}\)
Given: \(P = 1\), \(Q = e^{-x}\)
Formula: I.F. \(= e^x\); \(y\cdot\text{I.F.} = \int Q\cdot\text{I.F.}\,dx\)
Step 1: \(ye^x = \int e^{-x}e^x dx = x + C\)
Step 2: \(y(0) = 1\): \(1 = C\), so \(y = (x + 1)e^{-x}\)
Step 3: \(y(1) = \dfrac{2}{e}\)
Common mistake: \(\dfrac{1}{e}\) (A) drops the constant (\(y = xe^{-x}\)). \(2e\) (C) multiplies by \(e^x\) instead of dividing.
Key point: Here \(Q \times \text{I.F.} = 1\), which makes the integral easy.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\log x = \dfrac{1}{x}\) (\(x > 0\))
(B) \(\dfrac{d}{dx}a^x = a^x\log a\) (\(a > 0\))
(C) \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\cos^{-1}x = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - x^2}}\)
(D) \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\tan x = \sec^2 x\)
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C) only
Why: Only (C) is false: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\cos^{-1}x = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - x^2}}\).
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) are standard derivatives. Options (A), (B) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: The "co-" inverse functions have a minus sign in their derivatives.

questions.sub_topic: Rate of change of the perimeter of a square
questions.question: The side of a square increases at 3 cm/s. Its perimeter increases at:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(12\) cm/s
Given: \(\dfrac{da}{dt} = 3\)
Formula: \(P = 4a\), so \(\dfrac{dP}{dt} = 4\dfrac{da}{dt}\)
Step 1: \(4 \times 3 = 12\) cm/s
Common mistake: \(3\) cm/s (A) gives the rate of the side.
Key point: The perimeter changes four times as fast as the side.

questions.question: The vectors \(2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - 6\hat{k}\) and \(-4\hat{i} + \mu\hat{j} + 12\hat{k}\) are collinear. Then \(\mu\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(-6\)
Given: collinear means one vector is a scalar multiple of the other
Formula: \(\dfrac{-4}{2} = \dfrac{\mu}{3} = \dfrac{12}{-6}\)
Step 1: The ratio is \(-2\)
Step 2: \(\mu = 3 \times (-2) = -6\)
Common mistake: \(6\) (A) loses the sign of the ratio. \(-2\) (C) gives the ratio, not \(\mu\).
Key point: All three component ratios must be equal.

questions.question: The local maximum value of \(f(x) = x + \dfrac{1}{x}\) (\(x \ne 0\)) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(-2\)
Given: \(f'(x) = 1 - \dfrac{1}{x^2}\), \(f''(x) = \dfrac{2}{x^3}\)
Formula: local maximum where \(f' = 0\) and \(f'' < 0\)
Step 1: \(f'(x) = 0 \Rightarrow x = \pm 1\)
Step 2: \(f''(-1) = -2 < 0\): local maximum \(f(-1) = -2\)
Step 3: \(f''(1) = 2 > 0\): local minimum \(f(1) = 2\)
Common mistake: \(2\) (B) assumes the maximum must be the larger value; here the local maximum is less than the local minimum.
Key point: "Local" compares only with nearby values.

questions.sub_topic: Magnitude of a − b from the magnitude of a + b
questions.question: For vectors with \(|\vec{a}| = 3\), \(|\vec{b}| = 4\) and \(|\vec{a} + \vec{b}| = 5\), the value of \(|\vec{a} - \vec{b}|\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(5\)
Given: \(|\vec{a} + \vec{b}|^2 = 25\)
Formula: \(|\vec{a} \pm \vec{b}|^2 = |\vec{a}|^2 + |\vec{b}|^2 \pm 2\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}\)
Step 1: \(25 = 9 + 16 + 2\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} \Rightarrow \vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = 0\)
Step 2: \(|\vec{a} - \vec{b}|^2 = 9 + 16 - 0 = 25\), so \(|\vec{a} - \vec{b}| = 5\)
Common mistake: \(1\) (A) subtracts the magnitudes. \(7\) (B) adds them.
Key point: Square magnitudes to bring in the dot product.

questions.question: If \(y = \sin^{-1}x\) (\(-1 < x < 1\)), then \((1 - x^2)\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} - x\dfrac{dy}{dx}\) equals:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(0\)
Given: \(y' = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - x^2}}\), so \(\sqrt{1 - x^2}\,y' = 1\)
Formula: differentiate the product
Step 1: \(\sqrt{1 - x^2}\,y'' + y'\cdot\dfrac{-x}{\sqrt{1 - x^2}} = 0\)
Step 2: Multiply by \(\sqrt{1 - x^2}\): \((1 - x^2)y'' - xy' = 0\)
Common mistake: \(1\) (B) stops at \(\sqrt{1 - x^2}\,y' = 1\) without differentiating again.
Key point: Clear the square root before the second differentiation.

questions.question:
For \(A = \begin{bmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{bmatrix}\), match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) \(A + A^T\)
(B) \(A - A^T\)
(C) \(2A\)
(D) \(A^T\)

List-II
(I) \(\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\)
(II) \(\begin{bmatrix}1&3\\2&4\end{bmatrix}\)
(III) \(\begin{bmatrix}2&5\\5&8\end{bmatrix}\)
(IV) \(\begin{bmatrix}2&4\\6&8\end{bmatrix}\)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II)
Given: \(A^T = \begin{bmatrix}1&3\\2&4\end{bmatrix}\) (II)
Step 1: \(A + A^T = \begin{bmatrix}2&5\\5&8\end{bmatrix}\) (III), which is symmetric
Step 2: \(A - A^T = \begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\) (I), which is skew-symmetric
Step 3: \(2A = \begin{bmatrix}2&4\\6&8\end{bmatrix}\) (IV)
Common mistake: (A) swaps the sum and the difference. (C) swaps \(2A\) and \(A^T\). (D) swaps the difference and \(2A\).
Key point: \(A + A^T\) is symmetric and \(A - A^T\) is skew-symmetric.

questions.sub_topic: A 6, given the throw is even
questions.question: A die is thrown. Given that the number shown is even, the probability that it is 6 is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\dfrac{1}{3}\)
Given: \(F = \{2, 4, 6\}\), \(E = \{6\}\)
Formula: \(P(E \mid F) = \dfrac{n(E \cap F)}{n(F)}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{1}{3}\)
Common mistake: \(\dfrac{1}{6}\) (A) ignores the condition.
Key point: The condition shrinks the sample space to the even numbers.

questions.question: If \(\begin{vmatrix}x&2\\18&x\end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix}6&2\\18&6\end{vmatrix}\), then \(x\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(\pm 6\)
Given: left side \(x^2 - 36\); right side \(36 - 36 = 0\)
Formula: equate the two values
Step 1: \(x^2 - 36 = 0 \Rightarrow x^2 = 36\)
Step 2: \(x = \pm 6\)
Common mistake: (A) and (C) keep only one square root. \(36\) (B) is \(x^2\), not \(x\).
Key point: \(x^2 = a\) has two roots.

questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) \(\int \sec x\tan x\,dx\)
(B) \(\int \text{cosec}^2 x\,dx\)
(C) \(\int \dfrac{dx}{1 + x^2}\)
(D) \(\int a^x\,dx\)

List-II
(I) \(\dfrac{a^x}{\log a} + C\)
(II) \(\tan^{-1}x + C\)
(III) \(-\cot x + C\)
(IV) \(\sec x + C\)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
Why: Each is the reverse of a standard derivative: \((\sec x)' = \sec x\tan x\) (IV); \((-\cot x)' = \text{cosec}^2 x\) (III); \((\tan^{-1}x)' = \dfrac{1}{1 + x^2}\) (II); \(\left(\dfrac{a^x}{\log a}\right)' = a^x\) (I).
Why not the others: (A) swaps the first two. (B) swaps the second and third. (C) swaps the last two.
Key point: Check an integral by differentiating the answer.

questions.sub_topic: Estimate from a trend line with half-year coding
questions.question: For 4 years, coded \(x = -3, -1, 1, 3\), the data give \(\sum y = 80\), \(\sum xy = 40\) and \(\sum x^2 = 20\). The least squares trend value at \(x = 5\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(30\)
Given: \(n = 4\), \(\sum x = 0\)
Formula: \(a = \dfrac{\sum y}{n}\), \(b = \dfrac{\sum xy}{\sum x^2}\)
Step 1: \(a = 20\), \(b = 2\), so \(y = 20 + 2x\)
Step 2: At \(x = 5\): \(20 + 10 = 30\)
Common mistake: \(28\) (A) uses \(x = 4\), the next whole number, but with this coding the next year is \(x = 5\).
Key point: With an even number of years, codes go up in steps of 2.

questions.question: \(\displaystyle\int_0^3 e^{x/3}\,dx\) equals:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(3(e - 1)\)
Given: \(e^{ax}\) with \(a = \dfrac{1}{3}\)
Formula: \(\int e^{ax}dx = \dfrac{1}{a}e^{ax}\)
Step 1: \([3e^{x/3}]_0^3 = 3e - 3\)
Step 2: \(= 3(e - 1)\)
Common mistake: \(\dfrac{e - 1}{3}\) (C) multiplies by \(a\) instead of dividing. \(3e\) (B) forgets the lower limit.
Key point: Dividing by \(\dfrac{1}{3}\) means multiplying by 3.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Marginal revenue is \(\dfrac{dR}{dx}\).
(B) At the output where average cost is least, marginal cost equals average cost.
(C) Profit is greatest where \(MR = MC\) and the slope of \(MC\) exceeds the slope of \(MR\).
(D) Fixed cost changes as output changes.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) is the definition. (B) \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{C}{x}\right) = 0\) gives \(C' = \dfrac{C}{x}\). (C) This is the second-order condition for maximum profit.
Why not the others: (D) is false: fixed cost does not depend on output. Options (B) and (C) include (D); (A) leaves out (C).
Key point: Profit is maximised where \(P'(x) = 0\) and \(P''(x) < 0\).

questions.question: A perpetuity pays ₹500 every half-year. If money is worth 10% per annum compounded half-yearly, its present value is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹10,000
Given: \(R = 500\) per half-year, \(i = \dfrac{0.10}{2} = 0.05\) per half-year
Formula: PV \(= \dfrac{R}{i}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{500}{0.05} = 10{,}000\)
Common mistake: ₹5,000 (A) uses the annual rate 10%. ₹20,000 (C) doubles the payment and keeps the half-yearly rate.
Key point: The payment and the rate must refer to the same period.

questions.sub_topic: EMI for a one-year loan at 1% a month
questions.question: A loan of ₹1,00,000 is repaid in 12 monthly instalments at 12% per annum compounded monthly. Taking \((1.01)^{12} \approx 1.1268\), the EMI is about:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹8,885
Given: \(P = 1{,}00{,}000\), \(i = 0.01\), \(n = 12\)
Formula: EMI \(= \dfrac{Pi(1 + i)^n}{(1 + i)^n - 1}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{1{,}00{,}000 \times 0.01 \times 1.1268}{0.1268} = \dfrac{1126.8}{0.1268}\)
Step 2: \(\approx 8{,}886\), that is about ₹8,885
Common mistake: ₹9,333 (B) adds simple interest of ₹12,000 and divides by 12. ₹8,333 (C) ignores interest.
Key point: The reducing balance makes the EMI lower than the flat-rate figure.

questions.sub_topic: Poisson mean from two equal probabilities
questions.question: For a Poisson variable \(X\), \(P(X = 1) = P(X = 2)\). The mean of \(X\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(2\)
Given: \(P(X = r) = \dfrac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^r}{r!}\)
Formula: equate the two probabilities
Step 1: \(e^{-\lambda}\lambda = \dfrac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^2}{2}\)
Step 2: \(\lambda = \dfrac{\lambda^2}{2} \Rightarrow \lambda = 2\) (since \(\lambda > 0\))
Common mistake: \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) (B) inverts \(2! = 2\). \(1\) (A) cancels the factorial.
Key point: The mean of a Poisson distribution is \(\lambda\).

questions.question: The marginal cost is \(MC = 2x + 4\) and the fixed cost is ₹50. The total cost of producing 10 units is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹190
Given: \(MC = 2x + 4\), \(C(0) = 50\)
Formula: \(C(x) = \int MC\,dx\), constant from the fixed cost
Step 1: \(C(x) = x^2 + 4x + k\); \(C(0) = 50 \Rightarrow k = 50\)
Step 2: \(C(10) = 100 + 40 + 50 = 190\)
Common mistake: ₹140 (B) leaves out the fixed cost. ₹24 (C) is the marginal cost at \(x = 10\).
Key point: The constant of integration is the fixed cost.

questions.topic: Unit I: Numbers, Quantification and Numerical Applications
questions.question: The remainder when \(7^{100}\) is divided by 5 is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(1\)
Given: \(7 \equiv 2 \pmod 5\)
Formula: find a power of 2 that is \(\equiv 1 \pmod 5\)
Step 1: \(2^4 = 16 \equiv 1 \pmod 5\)
Step 2: \(7^{100} \equiv 2^{100} = (2^4)^{25} \equiv 1^{25} = 1 \pmod 5\)
Common mistake: \(2\) (B) reduces the base but forgets the power. \(4\) (C) uses \(2^2\).
Key point: Look for a cycle in the powers.

questions.sub_topic: t-statistic for a sample of nine
questions.question: A sample of 9 has mean 52 and standard deviation 3 (divisor \(n - 1\)). For \(H_0: \mu = 50\), the t-statistic is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(2\)
Given: \(n = 9\), \(\bar{x} = 52\), \(s = 3\), \(\mu = 50\)
Formula: \(t = \dfrac{\bar{x} - \mu}{s/\sqrt{n}}\)
Step 1: Standard error \(= \dfrac{3}{3} = 1\)
Step 2: \(t = \dfrac{2}{1} = 2\)
Common mistake: \(0.67\) (A) divides by \(s\). \(0.22\) (D) divides by \(s \times \sqrt{n}\).
Key point: Divide by \(s/\sqrt{n}\), not by \(s\).

questions.sub_topic: Moving averages and the least squares line
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) A five-yearly moving average gives no value for the first two and last two years.
(B) Moving averages smooth out short-term fluctuations.
(C) The least squares trend line passes through \((\bar{x}, \bar{y})\).
(D) A four-yearly moving average can be placed against a year without centring.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (D) only
Why: Only (D) is false: a four-yearly average falls between two years, so it must be centred.
Why not the others: (A) the first average belongs to year 3. (B) is the purpose of moving averages. (C) follows from \(a = \bar{y} - b\bar{x}\). Options (B), (C) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: Even-period moving averages need centring.

questions.topic: Unit I: Numbers, Quantification and Numerical Applications
questions.sub_topic: Race with a start and a speed ratio
questions.question: In a 500 m race, the speeds of A and B are in the ratio \(3 : 4\). A is given a start of 140 m. A wins by:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(20\) m
Given: A runs \(500 - 140 = 360\) m; speeds \(3 : 4\)
Formula: in the same time, distances are in the ratio of speeds
Step 1: While A runs 360 m, B runs \(360 \times \dfrac{4}{3} = 480\) m
Step 2: B is \(500 - 480 = 20\) m short when A finishes
Common mistake: \(40\) m (B) compares 360 with 400 instead of using the speed ratio correctly.
Key point: Compare distances covered in the same time.

questions.sub_topic: Depreciation as a percentage of cost
questions.question: A machine costs ₹80,000 and has a scrap value of ₹8,000 after 6 years. The annual straight-line depreciation as a percentage of cost is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(15\%\)
Given: cost ₹80,000, scrap ₹8,000, life 6 years
Formula: depreciation \(= \dfrac{\text{cost} - \text{scrap}}{\text{life}}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{72{,}000}{6} = ₹12{,}000\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{12{,}000}{80{,}000} = 15\%\)
Common mistake: \(16.67\%\) (D) is \(\dfrac{1}{6}\), which ignores the scrap value.
Key point: Subtract the scrap value before dividing by the life.

questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) Null hypothesis
(B) Alternative hypothesis
(C) Level of significance
(D) Degrees of freedom for a one-sample t-test with \(n = 20\)

List-II
(I) \(19\)
(II) The claim accepted when the null hypothesis is rejected
(III) A statement of no difference
(IV) The probability of rejecting the null hypothesis when it is true
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(III), (B)-(II), (C)-(IV), (D)-(I)
Why: \(H_0\) states no difference (III); \(H_1\) is accepted when \(H_0\) is rejected (II); the level of significance is the chance of wrongly rejecting a true \(H_0\) (IV); d.f. \(= 20 - 1 = 19\) (I).
Why not the others: (A) swaps the two hypotheses. (B) swaps the alternative hypothesis and the level of significance. (D) swaps the level of significance and the degrees of freedom.
Key point: The test is built around the null hypothesis.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The present value of a perpetuity is \(\dfrac{R}{i}\).
(B) Each EMI contains part of the interest and part of the principal.
(C) The straight-line method charges the same depreciation every year.
(D) CAGR is the simple average of the yearly growth rates.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A), (B) and (C) are standard definitions.
Why not the others: (D) is false: CAGR is the constant compound rate \(\left(\dfrac{\text{final}}{\text{initial}}\right)^{1/n} - 1\), not an arithmetic average. Options (B) and (C) include (D); (A) leaves out (C).
Key point: CAGR is a geometric, not arithmetic, average.

questions.sub_topic: Maximum profit from demand and cost functions
questions.question: The demand function is \(p = 100 - 2x\) and the cost function is \(C(x) = 20x + 100\). The maximum profit is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(700\)
Given: \(R(x) = px = 100x - 2x^2\)
Formula: \(P(x) = R(x) - C(x)\); \(P'(x) = 0\)
Step 1: \(P(x) = 80x - 2x^2 - 100\)
Step 2: \(P'(x) = 80 - 4x = 0 \Rightarrow x = 20\); \(P'' = -4 < 0\)
Step 3: \(P(20) = 1600 - 800 - 100 = 700\)
Common mistake: \(20\) (A) is the output. \(800\) (D) forgets the fixed cost of 100.
Key point: Build revenue from demand: \(R = p \times x\).

questions.question: If \(E(X) = 4\), then \(E(2X + 3)\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(11\)
Given: \(E(X) = 4\)
Formula: \(E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b\)
Step 1: \(2(4) + 3 = 11\)
Common mistake: \(8\) (A) forgets the constant. \(14\) (B) multiplies the constant by 2 as well.
Key point: Expectation is linear.

questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) Mean of a binomial distribution
(B) Variance of a binomial distribution
(C) Variance of a Poisson distribution
(D) Standard normal variate

List-II
(I) \(\lambda\)
(II) \(np\)
(III) \(\dfrac{X - \mu}{\sigma}\)
(IV) \(npq\)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(III)
Why: Binomial mean \(np\) (II) and variance \(npq\) (IV); a Poisson distribution has variance equal to its mean \(\lambda\) (I); \(Z = \dfrac{X - \mu}{\sigma}\) (III).
Why not the others: (A) swaps the binomial mean and variance. (B) swaps the binomial and Poisson variances. (C) swaps \(\lambda\) and \(Z\).
Key point: Binomial variance is less than its mean; Poisson variance equals its mean.

questions.sub_topic: Minimum cost on a triangular region
questions.question: The minimum value of \(Z = 200x + 500y\) subject to \(x + 2y \ge 10\), \(3x + 4y \le 24\), \(x, y \ge 0\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(2300\)
Given: the feasible region is a triangle
Formula: evaluate \(Z\) at each corner
Step 1: Intersection of \(x + 2y = 10\) and \(3x + 4y = 24\): doubling the first, \(2x + 4y = 20\), so \(x = 4\), \(y = 3\)
Step 2: Corners \((0, 5)\), \((4, 3)\), \((0, 6)\) give \(Z = 2500, 2300, 3000\)
Step 3: Minimum \(Z = 2300\) at \((4, 3)\)
Common mistake: \(2000\) (D) uses \((10, 0)\), which breaks \(3x + 4y \le 24\). \(2500\) (A) misses the intersection corner.
Key point: Check that each corner satisfies every constraint.

questions.question: Using Cramer's rule, the value of \(x\) satisfying \(3x - 2y = 4\) and \(x + y = 3\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(2\)
Given: \(D = \begin{vmatrix}3&-2\\1&1\end{vmatrix} = 3 + 2 = 5\)
Formula: \(x = \dfrac{D_x}{D}\)
Step 1: \(D_x = \begin{vmatrix}4&-2\\3&1\end{vmatrix} = 4 + 6 = 10\)
Step 2: \(x = \dfrac{10}{5} = 2\)
Common mistake: \(10\) (D) stops at \(D_x\). \(1\) (B) is the value of \(y\).
Key point: Replace the \(x\)-column by the constants.

questions.question: The value of \(\begin{vmatrix}5&3\\-2&4\end{vmatrix}\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(26\)
Given: \(a = 5\), \(b = 3\), \(c = -2\), \(d = 4\)
Formula: \(ad - bc\)
Step 1: \(20 - (3)(-2) = 20 + 6 = 26\)
Common mistake: \(14\) (A) subtracts 6 instead of adding it.
Key point: Subtracting a negative product adds it.

questions.question: If \(y = \log(2x + 1)\), then \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\dfrac{2}{2x + 1}\)
Given: outer \(\log u\), inner \(u = 2x + 1\)
Formula: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\log u = \dfrac{1}{u}\dfrac{du}{dx}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{1}{2x + 1} \times 2 = \dfrac{2}{2x + 1}\)
Common mistake: (A) forgets the derivative of the inner function.
Key point: Multiply by the derivative of what is inside the logarithm.

questions.question: For a binomial distribution with \(n = 12\) and \(p = \dfrac{1}{4}\), the variance is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(2.25\)
Given: \(n = 12\), \(p = \dfrac{1}{4}\), \(q = \dfrac{3}{4}\)
Formula: variance \(= npq\)
Step 1: \(12 \times \dfrac{1}{4} \times \dfrac{3}{4} = \dfrac{9}{4} = 2.25\)
Common mistake: \(3\) (B) is the mean \(np\). \(1.5\) (C) is the standard deviation.
Key point: Variance \(= np \times q\).

questions.sub_topic: Marginal cost at a given output
questions.question: For \(C(x) = 3x^2 + 5x + 7\), the marginal cost at \(x = 2\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(17\)
Given: \(C(x) = 3x^2 + 5x + 7\)
Formula: \(MC = C'(x) = 6x + 5\)
Step 1: \(MC(2) = 12 + 5 = 17\)
Common mistake: \(29\) (B) is \(C(2)\), the total cost.
Key point: Marginal cost is the derivative of total cost.

questions.sub_topic: Particular solution of a decay equation
questions.question: The solution of \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} + 2y = 0\) with \(y(0) = 5\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(y = 5e^{-2x}\)
Given: \(\dfrac{dy}{y} = -2\,dx\)
Formula: \(y = Ce^{-2x}\)
Step 1: \(y(0) = C = 5\)
Step 2: \(y = 5e^{-2x}\)
Common mistake: (A) loses the minus sign. (B) adds the constant instead of multiplying.
Key point: In \(y = Ce^{kx}\), the constant multiplies.

questions.sub_topic: Cube of I + A when A² = A
questions.question: \(A\) is a square matrix with \(A^2 = A\). Then \((I + A)^3\) equals:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(I + 7A\)
Given: \(A^2 = A\), so every power \(A^n = A\)
Formula: expand step by step (\(I\) and \(A\) commute)
Step 1: \((I + A)^2 = I + 2A + A^2 = I + 3A\)
Step 2: \((I + A)^3 = (I + 3A)(I + A) = I + A + 3A + 3A^2 = I + 7A\)
Common mistake: \(I + 3A\) (A) is only the square. \(I + 8A\) (C) treats it as \(I + 2^3A\).
Key point: Replace every \(A^2\) by \(A\) as you go.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) A corner point of a feasible region lies on at least two boundary lines.
(B) An LPP with an unbounded feasible region may still have a minimum.
(C) If two adjacent corners give the same maximum, every point on the segment joining them is optimal.
(D) The objective function of an LPP is always maximised, never minimised.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (D) only
Why: Only (D) is false: cost problems, such as diet problems, minimise the objective.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) are correct facts about corner points. Options (A), (B) and (C) name a true statement as false.
Key point: An LPP optimises: maximises or minimises.

questions.question: \(\displaystyle\int (3x + 2)^4\,dx\) equals:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\dfrac{(3x + 2)^5}{15} + C\)
Given: put \(t = 3x + 2\), \(dt = 3\,dx\)
Formula: \(\int t^4\dfrac{dt}{3} = \dfrac{t^5}{15}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{(3x + 2)^5}{15} + C\)
Common mistake: (A) forgets to divide by 3. (C) differentiates.
Key point: Divide by the coefficient of \(x\) inside the bracket.

questions.sub_topic: Probability above the mean of a normal variable
questions.question: \(X\) is normal with mean 60 and standard deviation 8. Then \(P(X > 60)\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(0.5\)
Given: \(\mu = 60\)
Formula: \(Z = \dfrac{60 - 60}{8} = 0\); \(P(Z > 0) = 0.5\)
Step 1: The normal curve is symmetric about the mean, so half the area lies above it
Common mistake: \(0.68\) (A) is the area within one standard deviation. \(0.34\) (C) is the area between the mean and one SD above it.
Key point: The mean splits the normal curve into two equal halves.

questions.sub_topic: Changing the time unit of a trend equation
questions.question: A trend equation for annual sales is \(y = 50 + 4x\), with \(x\) measured in half-years from the origin. Rewritten with \(x\) measured in years (same origin), it becomes:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(y = 50 + 8x\)
Given: 1 year = 2 half-years
Formula: replace \(x\) (half-years) by \(2x\) (years)
Step 1: \(y = 50 + 4(2x) = 50 + 8x\)
Common mistake: (A) halves the slope instead of doubling it. (B) also doubles the intercept, which applies only when the figures themselves are converted.
Key point: A longer time unit means a larger change per unit.

questions.topic: Unit I: Numbers, Quantification and Numerical Applications
questions.question: How many kg of sugar costing ₹40 per kg must be mixed with 30 kg of sugar costing ₹50 per kg so that the mixture costs ₹46 per kg?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(20\) kg
Given: cheaper ₹40, dearer ₹50, mean ₹46
Formula: \(\dfrac{\text{cheaper}}{\text{dearer}} = \dfrac{50 - 46}{46 - 40} = \dfrac{4}{6} = \dfrac{2}{3}\)
Step 1: Cheaper quantity \(= 30 \times \dfrac{2}{3} = 20\) kg
Step 2: Check: \(\dfrac{20 \times 40 + 30 \times 50}{50} = \dfrac{2300}{50} = 46\) ✓
Common mistake: \(45\) kg (C) inverts the ratio.
Key point: The difference opposite each price gives its share.

questions.sub_topic: Determinant, adjoint, inverse and transpose of one matrix
questions.question:
For \(A = \begin{bmatrix}2&1\\4&3\end{bmatrix}\), match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) \(|A|\)
(B) \(\text{adj}\,A\)
(C) \(A^{-1}\)
(D) \(A^T\)

List-II
(I) \(\begin{bmatrix}2&4\\1&3\end{bmatrix}\)
(II) \(2\)
(III) \(\dfrac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}3&-1\\-4&2\end{bmatrix}\)
(IV) \(\begin{bmatrix}3&-1\\-4&2\end{bmatrix}\)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(III), (D)-(I)
Step 1: \(|A| = 6 - 4 = 2\) (II)
Step 2: \(\text{adj}\,A = \begin{bmatrix}3&-1\\-4&2\end{bmatrix}\) (IV)
Step 3: \(A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{2}\,\text{adj}\,A\) (III)
Step 4: \(A^T = \begin{bmatrix}2&4\\1&3\end{bmatrix}\) (I)
Common mistake: (A) swaps the determinant and the adjoint. (B) swaps the adjoint and the inverse. (D) swaps the inverse and the transpose.
Key point: \(A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{|A|}\text{adj}\,A\).

questions.topic: Unit I: Numbers, Quantification and Numerical Applications
questions.sub_topic: Day of the week after 45 days
questions.question: Today is Monday. The day of the week 45 days from today will be:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Thursday
Given: days repeat every 7
Formula: \(45 \bmod 7\)
Step 1: \(45 = 6 \times 7 + 3\), so remainder 3
Step 2: Monday + 3 days = Thursday
Common mistake: Wednesday (A) counts Monday as the first of the 3 days.
Key point: Only the remainder on division by 7 matters.

questions.topic: Unit I: Numbers, Quantification and Numerical Applications
questions.sub_topic: Mixing equal amounts of two solutions
questions.question: Vessel P has milk and water in the ratio \(3 : 1\); vessel Q has them in the ratio \(1 : 1\). Equal quantities from the two vessels are mixed. The ratio of milk to water in the mixture is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(5 : 3\)
Given: milk fractions \(\dfrac{3}{4}\) in P and \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) in Q
Formula: with equal quantities, the milk fraction is the average
Step 1: Milk \(= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{3}{4} + \dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{5}{8}\); water \(= \dfrac{3}{8}\)
Step 2: Ratio \(5 : 3\)
Common mistake: \(4 : 2\) (A) adds the ratio terms \((3 + 1) : (1 + 1)\), which is valid only if the vessels' total parts were equal. (D) gives water : milk.
Key point: Convert ratios to fractions of the whole before mixing.

questions.topic: Unit I: Numbers, Quantification and Numerical Applications
questions.sub_topic: Solving a rational inequality by signs
questions.question: The solution set of \(\dfrac{x - 2}{x + 3} > 0\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(x < -3\) or \(x > 2\)
Given: critical points \(x = 2\) and \(x = -3\)
Formula: a quotient is positive when numerator and denominator have the same sign
Step 1: Both positive: \(x > 2\)
Step 2: Both negative: \(x < -3\)
Common mistake: (A) is where the quotient is negative. (B) misses the case where both are negative.
Key point: Test the sign on each interval between the critical points.

questions.sub_topic: Mean of the sampling distribution of the mean
questions.question: Samples of size 64 are drawn from a population with mean 50. The mean of the sampling distribution of the sample mean is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(50\)
Given: \(\mu = 50\), \(n = 64\)
Formula: \(E(\bar{X}) = \mu\)
Step 1: \(50\)
Common mistake: \(\dfrac{50}{8}\) (A) divides by \(\sqrt{n}\), which applies to the standard error, not the mean.
Key point: The sample mean is centred on the population mean.
